reading.body:
AI risk is being priced from live physical telemetry rather than claims history, because the exposure is too new to have a loss record.

The pattern is that the policy is bound to the building. Thermals, humidity and load variation adjust premiums. Temperature or power crossing a threshold settles a claim automatically, with no loss adjustment. Policy limits scale with active GPU consumption and deployment footprint. Underwriting itself runs on vision models and sensor analytics applied to the data centre. None of this depends on a claims record, because there is not one to depend on.

For AI this matters because the quantities that price cover are the quantities that constrain compute. Power, temperature and GPU consumption appear as underwriting inputs, as payout triggers and as the basis for limits, so the grid and the cooling plant become variables an insurer watches rather than only build costs. Two mechanisms address a risk ordinary property cover cannot reach. Correlated accumulation models the case where one foundational model serves millions of businesses and a single failure becomes a systemic loss. Synthetic loss scenarios price failure modes that have never occurred. Governance also becomes a price signal, through red teaming as a condition of cover, maturity scoring for discounts, and third party safety ratings that determine underwriting eligibility.

What the data does not cover is scale. There are no premiums, no loss figures, no named insurers, no dates and no indication of how widely any of these mechanisms are in force. It describes how AI risk can be underwritten, not how much of it is. It cannot say whether a parametric trigger has ever paid out, or whether a correlated accumulation model has been tested against a real event. Read it as a map of the instruments, not as evidence of the market.
